title: Splice Two Sorted Chains
statement:
You get the heads of two singly linked lists, a and b. Each list is sorted in non-decreasing order.

Combine them into one sorted list by relinking their nodes, and return its head. Equal values may come in either order. Either list may be empty.

Lists are written as arrays: [1, 5] is 1 → 5. An empty list is null (shown as [] in examples).

examples.why: Both 5s stay. When a runs out after 8, the leftover 10 from b has to be attached as a whole.
With one list empty, the answer is simply the other list.
The head of the result can come from either list, so you cannot just return a.

constraints: Both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: The smallest value overall is at the front of one of the two lists. Which one?
Repeatedly take the smaller of the two fronts and attach it to the end of your result. What happens when one list runs out?
Start the result with a dummy node so the very first attach is no special case. When one list is empty, hang the whole other list on the tail in one step.

explain.intuition:
This is the merge step of merge sort. Two sorted queues, and you always take the smaller front. Because both lists are sorted, the smaller front is the smallest value that is left anywhere, so taking it can never be a mistake.

With linked lists you do not copy anything: you just relink the node you took onto the tail of the result. A dummy node in front of the result removes the "is the result still empty?" check, and you return dummy.next. Once one list runs out, the other one is already sorted and already linked, so a single pointer attaches all of it.
steps: While both a and b are non-null, pick the one with the smaller value (either one on a tie).
Set tail.next to that node, move that list forward, and move tail to the node.
When the loop ends, set tail.next = a ?? b to attach whatever is left.
pitfalls: Forgetting the leftover part. The loop stops as soon as one list is empty, and the other list's remaining nodes are dropped.
Returning dummy instead of dummy.next, which adds a fake 0 to the front.
Recursive merging: it is elegant, but it recurses once per node, which overflows the stack on long lists in Python.

solutions.title: Collect, sort, rebuild
solutions.idea: Dump every value into an array, sort it and build a new list. It works, but it ignores that the inputs were already sorted and allocates new nodes.

solutions.title: Dummy head and splice
solutions.idea: Always attach the smaller front node to the tail of the result. A dummy node in front avoids special-casing the first attach.

followups: Merge k sorted lists instead of two. Does merging them one by one stay fast?
The lists are sorted in descending order instead. What is the smallest change to the code?
